title: Shortest routes in a road network
intro: Eight towns, A to H, are joined by the two-way roads in the table (distances in km). There are no other roads.
clues: A route from one town to another never visits a town twice.

questions.stem: What is the length of the shortest route from A to H?
why: The shortest route is A-C-F-G-H: 4 + 8 + 3 + 4 = 19 km.
Next come A-C-D-F-G-H and A-D-F-G-H at 20 km each, and A-C-F-H at 21 km.

questions.stem: How many different routes from A to H have a length of at most 22 km?
why: By length: 19 km (A-C-F-G-H); 20 km (A-C-D-F-G-H, A-D-F-G-H); 21 km (A-C-F-H); 22 km (A-C-D-F-H, A-D-F-H).
Every other route is at least 23 km (A-B-E-G-H, A-C-D-G-H, A-D-G-H). 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 6.

questions.stem: If the road F-G is closed, what is the length of the shortest route from A to H?
why: Every route using F-G goes, including the three shortest.
The best left is A-C-F-H: 4 + 8 + 9 = 21 km. A-C-D-F-H and A-D-F-H are 22 km, and routes through E or D-G at least 23 km.

questions.stem: What is the length of the shortest route from A to H that passes through E?
why: A route through E has an A-to-E part (at least 13 km, A-B-E) and an E-to-H part (at least 10 km, E-G-H).
A-B-E-G-H is exactly 13 + 10 = 23 km.

questions.stem: A long-term repair adds 2 km to the length of every road. What is now the length, in km, of the shortest route from A to H?
why: Each route gains 2 km per road, so routes with fewer roads gain less. A-C-F-G-H (4 roads) becomes 27; A-C-F-H (3 roads) becomes 21 + 6 = 27.
The other 3-road routes become 28 (A-D-F-H) and 29 (A-D-G-H); every other route was at least 20 km with 4 or more roads, so is now at least 28. The shortest is 27 km.

steps: Find the shortest distance to each town from A, nearest first: C 4, B 6 (via C would be 7), D 9, F 12 (via C), E 13 (via B), G 15 (via F), H 19 (via G).
Trace H back the way it was reached: H from G, G from F, F from C, C from A. The shortest route is A-C-F-G-H, 19 km.
For the questions that count routes, list them by length (19, 20, 20, 21, 22, 22, then 23) instead of starting again. A closed road or an extra charge changes only the routes that use it.

diagram.note: Each town shows its shortest distance from A in km; the bold roads are the shortest route to H.

title: A delivery van and a table of predecessors
intro: A delivery van travels from the depot S to the market M through a chain of towns P, Q, R, T, U and V. It may reach a town only from the towns listed against it (its predecessors), and the table gives the travel time in hours from each. A route is a complete sequence of towns from S to M.

tables.caption: Where each town can be reached from (travel time in hours)
head: Town
Can be reached from

clues: The van never visits a town twice and never goes backwards.

questions.stem: What is the minimum travel time from S to M?
why: Earliest arrivals, each the best over its predecessors: P 2; Q min(3, 2 + 2) = 3; R min(6, 4) = 4; T min(7, 6) = 6; U min(9, 7) = 7; V min(9, 9) = 9; M min(11, 10) = 10 hours.

questions.stem: How many different routes from S to M take at most 11 hours?
why: 10 hours: S-Q-R-T-U-V-M and S-Q-R-T-V-M. 11 hours: S-P-Q-R-T-U-V-M, S-P-Q-R-T-V-M, S-Q-R-T-U-M, S-Q-T-U-V-M and S-Q-T-V-M.
Every other route takes 12 hours or more. 2 + 5 = 7.

questions.stem: The van must halt at R for 1.5 hours (a halt at R affects only routes that go through R). What is the new minimum travel time from S to M?
why: Routes through R take 1.5 hours longer, so the best of them becomes 11.5 hours.
Without R, T is reached at 3 + 4 = 7 at best, and S-Q-T-V-M takes 3 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 11 hours. The minimum is 11.

questions.stem: If town T is closed, how many different routes from S to M remain?
why: Without T, every route must go through R and then U (V can then be reached only from U).
To R: S-Q-R, S-P-Q-R or S-P-R. From R: R-U-M or R-U-V-M. 3 × 2 = 6 routes.

questions.stem: Now suppose the van also halts for 30 minutes in every town it passes through (but not at S or M). What is the minimum total time from S to M in minutes?
why: S-Q-R-T-V-M: 10 hours plus 4 halts of half an hour = 12 hours = 720 minutes.

Every route takes at least 10 hours; the 3-town routes take at least 11 hours of travel (12.5 with halts), and any route through 4 or more towns gains at least 2 hours. Only S-Q-R-T-V-M reaches 12 hours.

steps: Work out the earliest arrival at each town, in order: each is the smallest of (a predecessor's time + the leg). S 0, P 2, Q 3, R 4, T 6, U 7, V 9, M 10.
Trace M back: M from V (9 + 1), and V from T (6 + 3) or U (7 + 2), both 9. Two routes take 10 hours: S-Q-R-T-V-M and S-Q-R-T-U-V-M.
There are 21 routes in all, 2 of 10 hours and 5 of 11. For a halt or a closed town, change only the routes that use it.

diagram.note: Each town shows its earliest arrival from S; the van moves left to right. Bold roads make up the two 10-hour routes.

title: A bus timetable with connection rules
intro: Five towns, A to E, are linked by ten daily bus services, each running non-stop between two towns at the times in the table (24-hour clock). The first bus can be taken at any time after the traveller is ready; a traveller ready at 06:00 can take any service.
clues: A traveller who changes bus at a town needs at least 10 minutes between arriving and the next bus's departure.
A traveller never visits a town twice.

questions.stem: A traveller at A is ready to leave at 06:00 and wants to reach E as early as possible. At what time does the traveller reach E?
why: Bus 1 reaches B at 06:50; Bus 5 leaves B at 07:15, 25 minutes later, and reaches E at 09:10.
Nothing arrives earlier: the next best itineraries arrive at 09:30.

questions.stem: How many different itineraries (sequences of buses, with every transfer at least 10 minutes) take a traveller ready at 06:00 from A to E?
why: Others fail: 1 + 4 + 6 has 5 minutes at C; 2 + 10 + 5 reaches B after Bus 5 has gone; 2 + 6 + 9 reaches D after Bus 9 leaves; 1 + 4 + 10 and 2 + 10 + 4 revisit a town. 6 itineraries.

questions.stem: Bus 1 is cancelled. A traveller ready at 06:00 at A again wants to reach E as early as possible. At what time does the traveller reach E?
why: Without Bus 1 nobody reaches B in time for Bus 5 (Bus 10 reaches B at 08:30).
The best left is Bus 2 to C (07:40), then Bus 7 at 08:10, reaching E at 09:30.

questions.stem: What is the largest minimum transfer time, in whole minutes, for which a traveller ready at 06:00 can still reach E by 09:10?
why: Only Bus 1 then Bus 5 reaches E by 09:10. Its transfer at B runs from 06:50 to 07:15: 25 minutes.
The connection works for any minimum transfer time up to 25 minutes.

questions.stem: A hail storm makes every bus arrive 10 minutes later than the timetable shows (departures are unchanged, and the 10-minute transfer rule still applies). How many minutes after 06:00 does the earliest possible arrival at E occur?
why: Bus 1 now reaches B at 07:00, still in time for Bus 5 at 07:15, which reaches E at 09:20.
That is 3 hours 20 minutes = 200 minutes after 06:00; nothing arrives earlier.

steps: Earliest arrivals by one bus from A: B 06:50 (Bus 1), C 07:40 (Bus 2), D 08:30 (Bus 3).
Add one change, 10 minutes or more. From B (06:50) Bus 5 at 07:15 is fine and reaches E at 09:10, the earliest. From C (07:40) Bus 7 reaches E at 09:30; from D, Bus 8 at 09:40.
For a cancelled or late bus, or a new transfer rule, remove or shift only the buses involved and check again the changes they feed.

diagram.note: Each town shows the earliest arrival from A, ready at 06:00. Bold: Bus 1 then Bus 5.

title: Connecting seven villages at lowest cost
intro: Seven villages, A to G, are to be linked by new roads so that every village can be reached from every other. The survey allows only the twelve roads in the table, with the building cost of each in lakh of rupees.

clues: The government builds exactly the roads needed to connect all seven villages with no unnecessary road, 6 roads in all, at the lowest total cost.

questions.stem: What is the minimum total cost, in lakh of rupees, of connecting all seven villages?
why: Take roads cheapest first, skipping any that would close a loop: A-B (4), D-E (4), B-C (5), C-D (5), E-G (5). These join every village but F.
F's cheapest road is D-F or F-G, both 6. Total 4 + 4 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 6 = 29.

questions.stem: In how many different ways can the cheapest network be built (two networks are different if they use different sets of roads)?
why: The five roads A-B, D-E, B-C, C-D and E-G are forced. F then joins by D-F or by F-G, both 6: two cheapest networks.

questions.stem: The road D-E is washed away and can no longer be built. What is the new minimum total cost?
why: Without D-E take A-B, B-C, C-D and E-G (19). Three groups remain: {A, B, C, D}, {E, G} and {F}.
D-F (6) and F-G (6) join all three for 12; any other pair costs more (C-E is 8). Total 31.

questions.stem: How many roads are included in every cheapest network?
why: A-B, B-C, C-D, D-E and E-G are in both cheapest networks; only F's road differs. 5 roads.

questions.stem: Because of a land deal, the road B-E (cost 9) must be built. What is the minimum total cost, in lakh of rupees, of a network that includes B-E?
why: Start with B-E (9), then cheapest first: A-B (4), D-E (4), B-C (5). C-D now closes a loop (C and D are joined through B-E), so skip it. E-G (5).
F costs 6 (D-F or F-G). Total 9 + 4 + 4 + 5 + 5 + 6 = 33.

steps: List the roads by cost: A-B 4, D-E 4, B-C 5, C-D 5, E-G 5, A-C 6, D-F 6, F-G 6, then 7, 7, 8, 9. Take each in turn unless it would close a loop; this always gives the cheapest network.
The first five, A-B, D-E, B-C, C-D and E-G, join every village except F, for 23. A-C (6) is skipped: A and C are already joined through B.
F is reached by D-F or by F-G, both 6, so there are two cheapest networks, each costing 29. At every tie, count the choices.

diagram.note: Costs in lakh of rupees. Bold roads are built; F needs only one of its two bold roads.

title: A courier tour through six towns
intro: A courier starts at the depot in town P and must deliver a parcel in each of the other five towns, Q, R, S, T and U. The shortest road distances between the towns are in the table, in km. A route is the order in which the five towns are visited after P; its length is the sum of the five distances along it.
clues: The courier visits every town exactly once and stops in the last town; the courier does not return to P.

questions.stem: What is the length of the shortest route?
why: P-Q-S-R-T-U is 1 + 5 + 6 + 4 + 3 = 19 km, the shortest of the 24 routes that start P-Q.
A route not starting P-Q has a first leg of at least 6, enters Q by at least 5, and has three more legs of at least 3: at least 20 km.

questions.stem: How many different routes have a length of at most 23 km?
why: 19 km: P-Q-S-R-T-U. 20 km: P-Q-R-T-U-S and P-Q-S-U-T-R. 22 km: P-Q-R-S-U-T and P-Q-S-R-U-T. 23 km: P-Q-R-S-T-U and P-S-Q-R-T-U.
Every other route is at least 24 km. 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7.

questions.stem: The road between P and Q is closed, so the courier cannot start with the leg P-Q (every other leg works as before). What is the length of the shortest route now?
why: The best route starting P-S is P-S-Q-R-T-U = 6 + 5 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 23 km.
Starting P-R gives at least 25 km, and P-T or P-U at least 30 km.

questions.stem: What is the length of the shortest route that ends in town Q?
why: Q cannot come first, so the first leg is at least 6 km. The best are P-R-T-U-S-Q = 6 + 4 + 3 + 7 + 5 = 25 and P-S-U-T-R-Q = 6 + 7 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 25.
All other routes ending at Q are at least 29 km.

questions.stem: For each possible last town (Q, R, S, T and U) find the length of the shortest route that ends there. What is the sum of these five lengths?
why: Ending at U: P-Q-S-R-T-U, 19. At R: P-Q-S-U-T-R, 20. At S: P-Q-R-T-U-S, 20. At T: P-Q-R-S-U-T or P-Q-S-R-U-T, 22. At Q: 25.

steps: A route has 5 legs, so there are 5! = 120 routes, 24 for each first town after P. Group them by the first town.
First town Q: Q is only 1 km from P, and this group holds the best routes. The shortest is P-Q-S-R-T-U, 19 km; the next are 20, 20, 22, 22 and 23.
Best of the other groups: first town S, 23 km (P-S-Q-R-T-U); R, 25 km (P-R-T-U-S-Q); T or U, 30 km.
Each question crosses out the routes its rule forbids and reads the first one left.

diagram.note: The best route in each group, by the first town after P.
